newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi crops improve but food deficit remains.
newsitem.headline: Burundi crops improve but food deficit remains.

text.p: People in Burundi will have less food to eat this year despite a small increase in production, the U.N. said on Tuesday.

A joint report released by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) found agriculture picking up as security, the supply of inputs and the weather improved in the war-torn nation.
"The mission found that overall, the season benefited from improved security, input supply and better weather conditions," said the report.
Fighting between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels in the ethnically divided nation has disrupted economic activity as a whole.

The report obtained by Reuters says the poverty-stricken country needs to import more food and faces a reduction in per capita consumption despite an increase of almost one percent rise in total food output in 1977.
Food security in has nosedived since 1993, when production ground to a halt as civil war triggered large-scale movements of refugees within the country.
Production in 1997 will still be four percent below the average for 1988-1993.
The mission estimates yields from the second of 1997's three harvests will be four percent up on last year.
But the results of the third harvest will hinge on security, weather conditions and supply of inputs, all deeply uncertain factors.
The latest harvest was stunted by a late distribution of fertiliser, the low quantity and quality of seeds and a lack of pesticides.
The report says Burundi will not be able to import enough food to plug the gap between production and population growth.

Assuming a mid-1997 population of 5.98 million and average consumption requirements based on reduced amounts available during 1994-96, Burundi will have to import the equivalent of 128,000 tonnes of cereals.
But the imports needed, in the form of cereals, pulses, roots, tubers, bananas and plaintains, are well above the amount Burundi can realistically hope for.

Commercial imports are forecast at 3,000 tonnes of cereals and 12,000 tonnes of pulses. This leaves shortfalls of 17,000 tonnes of cereals, 44,000 tonnes of pulses and 52,000 tonnes (cereals equivalent) of roots, tubers, bananas and plantains.
As of June 30, 1997 food aid distributed by WFP amounted to 6,000 tonnes of cereals and 3,000 tonnes of pulses.
A further 16,000 tonnes of cereals and 5,000 tonnes of pulses are expected to be provided by the end of this year.
